Unemployment & Labor Markets

14 pts

3 · Comparing the labor markets

Mexico's headline unemployment rate is lower than the U.S. most years and is, in theory, consistently stronger, which surprises people. The economic point is that it's not because Mexico's labor market is stronger, but more likely because Mexico has a large informal sector and weak unemployment benefits, so people can not afford unemployment. They take informal work instead. That's exactly what the youth indicator helps expose: youth get pushed into informal and precarious work rather than showing up as unemployed. Over time, both countries remain stable outside major shocks. The U.S. spikes hard during recessions; 2008 and the 2020 COVID drop are the obvious ones; and then falls back down, while Mexico's rate moves less dramatically but tends to stay elevated a little longer after each hit. That gap is part of the story: when jobs disappear in Mexico, people don't stop working; they shift into informal work, so the unemployment number barely moves. The youth rate makes this clearer than the headline number, since younger workers are the first ones pushed into that unstable work and their unemployment runs noticeably higher than the overall rate in both countries.

Money, Banking & Currency

12 pts

1 · Currency & central bank

1. The currency that Mexico uses is the Mexican Peso (MXN) and the central bank is the Banco de Mexico (Banxico)

2 · Visual

3 · Interest rate comparison

4 · Money & banking explained

4. The biggest thing that stands out comparing these two is the gap; Mexico’s interest rates sit well above U.S. Rates every year on the chart, and it’s usually not close. Mexico runs several percentage points higher. The reason for this is Mexico historically dealt with higher and less stable inflation than the U.S., so Banxico must keep rates up to keep prices under control and to keep the peso attractive to investors. Higher rates make it more worthwhile to have pesos against foreign currency. You also see both graphs move in the same general direction: both drop hard around 2008 and again during COVID when both central banks cut rates to prop up their economies, then both climb up through 2022-2023 as inflation rises. Mexico is also able to keep rates higher because they historically have different issues than the US when it comes to unemployment.

6

International Trade & Finance

20 pts

4 · Major exports, imports & trading partners

5 · Trade & finance explained

Mexico’s economy is built around trade in ways the U.S. isn’t. Exports are a huge part of the Mexican economy when compared to the U.S. economy; the U.S. is sitting around 10 percent, while Mexico’s GDP has become more and more dependent on exports, specifically the U.S. More than 80 percent of everything Mexico exports goes to the US which makes the two economies almost one connected supply chain rather than two separate ones. Mexico tends to run a trade surplus with the US, mostly because so much of what it exports is actually foreign companies building cars, electronics, and machinery in Mexican factories and then shipping the finished product north. The exchange rate matters a lot here. When the peso weakens against the dollar, Mexican exports get cheaper and more competitive, which is good for exporters and the factories that employ people. It makes, however, imported goods and anything priced in dollars more expensive for regular consumers. A weaker peso also means the money workers send home in the US is worth more once it's converted. In the end, Mexico gets real benefits from trade and cheap currency, but it also leaves Mexico heavily dependent on one partner and vulnerable whenever US demand slows down.

7

Conclusion

5 pts

When looking at Mexico, it reveals an economy with some real strengths but also many vulnerabilities. Its biggest strengths are that it’s a major producer of vehicles, electronics, and machinery, and its location right next to the world’s largest consumer market gives it an advantage a lot of countries don’t have. Remittances from workers in the US add another source of income that helps support households. Those same strengths are also where the challenges come from. More than 80 percent of Mexico's exports go to one country, which makes the economy heavily dependent on US demand. Not only that, but many trends across all aspects of the economy are tied together.
